extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and newsroom editors (working journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical standards and do's/don'ts for reporters about source handling, confidentiality, neutrality, and sensitive beats (war, reformers, advertisers). Advice covers when to accept or refuse 'off the record' requests, protecting sources' identities, avoiding bias, and publishing responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify what is 'off the record'
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to find out explicitly what items were off the record has ruined many a good story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ask and confirm exactly which statements or items the speaker considers not usable; treat 'off the record' as applying only to the explicitly designated bits. Example: reporter discovers only three bits are not usable and everything else approved for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for permission to restate in private
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker may be willing to make public what he said, but not in speech form; a reporter can request a private interview to repeat the statements without reference to the original setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a speaker objects to the original public context (e.g., 'I was their guest, and I have to think of that'), offer a private interview and use that material if the speaker agrees (example: remove mention of Rotary Club).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse misuse of 'off the record' to conceal public interest information
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Off the record' sometimes is used to tie up information that should be of free and open access; public officials may adopt it to silence controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source repeatedly labels answers 'off the record' to avoid public scrutiny, interrupt and say you won't accept more 'off the record' answers and ask them to speak openly or stop. Breaking up such hush-hush can be legitimate duty to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect anonymity while still reporting the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Very often a person of prominence is willing to talk as long as his name is not used; the story can protect him by deleting his name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anonymous attribution or phrases like 'sources close to city hall' or 'city hall observers predicted' to report content while masking identity; paraphrase to avoid direct naming when the speaker requests anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not punish a source for refusing to discuss private matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Reticent interviewees are not to be punished for taciturnity about personal matters; avoid pillorying them in the story for refusing to confirm or deny private allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source declines to answer private/personal questions, do not frame the story as condemning their silence. Distinguish private from public matters and avoid wording that suggests blanket clamminess when silence applied only to a specific question.

rubrics_metrics.name: When public concern is at stake, report precise refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject comes into public concern, the reporter is fully within the proprieties if he recounts the subject's refusal to discuss what he did officially; in fairness, the reporter will give the precise question that the subject refused to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the exact question refused rather than vague paraphrases such as 'would not explain why he voted as he did,' which can mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep promises and confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: When he does accept a confidence, the reporter must adhere to it regardless of how badly he may be beaten by the opposition paper. A promise made is a promise to be kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never break an explicit promise of confidentiality; breaking confidences ruins a reporter's reputation and sources, described as 'professional suicide.' The long-term loss of trust and sources outweighs short-term gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: If information is confirmed elsewhere, revisit source before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: One man cannot bottle up information available through other sources; if another equally qualified source makes the information public, the reporter should return to the original source to explain that the story will run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a piece of information the source wanted kept confidential appears from another qualified source, go back and explain to avoid charges of breaking confidence; this protects both the reporter and the paper (example: Durkee/Boston store sale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish private social conversation without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: What he hears in his social contacts is not for publication; only when the person has been asked whether he is willing to have the story run is it available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you hear newsworthy remarks off-duty (e.g., at a bridge game), seek explicit permission before using them. Using off-duty remarks will make people 'mum' and dry up future sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect private vs. public meeting distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not allowable to try to break down the distinction between a private and a public meeting; the private nature of a meeting governs whether its contents may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if dozens heard a private club speech, don't publish its content if the meeting was private and attendees were not open to the public (example: Lions Club). Violating this will blacklist the reporter among community sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid news coverage tailored to editorial positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The accusation that the news columns are warped to agree with the editorial page is misplaced; editors do not write editorials before knowing the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain independence between news reporting and editorial advocacy; news should be reported for its own facts, not shaped to fit an editorial agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist advertiser coercion unless legal constraints apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish the news despite advertiser threats unless legal concerns (e.g., libel) prevent publication; papers often must carry stories even when advertisers object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If advertisers threaten withdrawal, stand by legitimate reporting. If there is truly no story or a libel risk, exercise caution; but do not censor valid news simply due to pressure. Examples show papers carrying arrests despite advertiser threats when story is legally available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize fueling local wartime antagonism (war reporting neutrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must do their utmost to keep the local news from fostering and fanning the antagonisms the war is breeding; avoid inflaming passions and prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize readers' strong partisan reactions; avoid phrasing or selection that fans hysteria. Aim for a sane view and avoid making a foreign war 'ours' by incendiary local coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report opposing or controversial views fairly and without insinuation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a speaker defends an unpopular cause, the reporter must present that speech fairly, without comment, and without insinuation or compression that twists meanings and ignores contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sly wording that implies the speaker personally endorses every viewpoint heard (examples: 'defended the Hun argument' or misattributing others' views as the speaker's own). Preserve context and avoid editorializing in news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with atrocity stories and hearsay
rubrics_metrics.description: Too often the reporter manhandled letters and presented hearsay atrocity claims as the truth rather than as one soldier's or correspondent's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify atrocity claims and make clear when material is secondhand or hearsay. Example contrast: don't convert 'we have heard that the Germans are crucifying prisoners' into a lead stating that German troops have crucified prisoners as an established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying war vocabulary/metaphors to unrelated news
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must avoid lugging the war vocabulary into other news; war words, used in nonwar stories, dilute and may be in poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gratuitous metaphors like 'torpedoed,' 'Blitzkrieg,' 'Siegfried lines,' or calling gatherings 'concentrations' when not discussing the war. Such usage can be incongruous, insensitive, and overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying espionage or foreign sympathies without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The police reporter should be unswervingly cautious about stories that directly or by implication link anyone to a foreign cause or espionage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reporting rumor as suspicion; do not state or imply espionage connections based on gossip or absence. Wrongful implication can harm individuals for months or years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present reformers and minorities impartially
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must not let personal hostility toward reformers affect impartial coverage; a minority has the right to present and work for its aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if reformers are eccentric or 'utopiacs,' they are entitled to fair and objective reporting. Avoid pejorative language and let readers judge, not the reporter's animus (example: Mr. Deems/Anti-Tobacco League).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise wording to avoid misleading impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: To say 'The senator would not explain why he voted as he did' gives a different impression than giving the precise question he refused to answer; vague wording can be glaringly inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing a subject's silence or refusal, include the exact question or context so readers understand the scope of the refusal and are not misled about the subject's overall cooperativeness.
